title: Nikole Hannah-Jones failed her daughter and learned absolutely nothing from it olutely-nothing-from-it/
author: Isaac Schorr
summary: Isaac Schorr argues that Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay is an unwitting admission of how one-trick ideologues harm those closest to them. He contrasts her 2024 declaration that her daughter was worth no more than any other child with her new regret, but says she still blames racism, segregation, and school choice rather than confronting accountability. Schorr points to P.S. 307's $52,000 per-pupil spending and low student-teacher ratio, compared with the far cheaper, successful district he attended, to argue that money and clout cannot fix bad schools. He blames New York's Board of Regents, appointed by a union-aligned legislature, for removing accountability, including exam requirements for graduation. His prescription runs from administrators and the Regents to parents and students themselves, all of whom must expect more.
points: Schorr contrasts Hannah-Jones's 2024 insistence she made the right choice with her 2026 regret.
He argues her essay still leans on the same explanations of racism, segregation, and school choice.
P.S. 307 spends almost twice per pupil what Schorr's successful home district spends, with a similar ratio.
The Board of Regents is portrayed as unaccountable and focused on eliminating standards such as graduation exams.
He insists parents and students must also take responsibility for academic commitment.
quotes: One-trick monomaniacs don’t just bore their audience, they hurt those closest to them with their narcissistic need to prove themselves right.
Indeed — but Hannah-Jones is the kind of sinner who attends confession only to make a mockery of it after leaving the booth.
No amount of money or personal clout of the kind Hannah-Jones thought she was bringing to the table is going to turn bad schools around.
Rather than try to hold schools and teachers to higher standards, the board spends its time getting rid of anything resembling accountability.
New York deserves a system built for its students, not for the low-performing, no-show teachers and administrators described by Hannah-Jones.
They fail because administrators, teachers, policymakers and parents fail them — usually by expecting too little of them.
